`send_message`, packaged: a blank @text@ with no @files@ posts nothing (a quiet protocol's silence);

declarations.documentation:
Serve a channel forever, delivering each incoming `message` to @deliver_to@ as one `message` value —
shaped like `time.watch` / `google_calendar.watch` so it composes under `parallel [ … ]`. The bot's own
posts (and other bots') are not delivered, so replying from @deliver_to@ cannot loop.

@author@ on the delivered message is the sender's raw Slack user id (an opaque `U…` id, but drawn from a
workspace's small, guessable space); a plain digest of one is dictionary-reversible, so pass it through
`author_tag` before letting it leave the program, e.g. as an AI provider's abuse-attribution tag.

Delivery is AT-LEAST-ONCE, which is where this differs from the Discord twin's neither-guarantee: Slack
acknowledges every event individually and re-sends one whose acknowledgement was lost to a dropped
socket, so a message can be REPEATED but not missed. No dedup memory is kept here, so a bot that must
not act twice dedupes on its own.

@deliver_to@'s own argument is named @value@, which is what changed in 0.4.0 and part of why it is a
breaking change. Argument names are STRUCTURAL in Katari — a callback is passed by name, so a callback
declared `(message: slack.message)` was accepted here and REJECTED by `gmail.watch` / `poll.subscribe`,
which name theirs @value@ as the prelude's primary-argument convention says. The chat twins were the only
holdouts, so the same agent could not be handed to a mail watch and a channel watch without an adapter
that renamed one word. Rename the callback's parameter to @value@ (the type is unchanged) and
`deliver_to = handler` keeps working everywhere.

declarations.documentation:
Post @prompt@ with @controls@ under it and BLOCK until someone in the channel answers, returning the
`answer` that control produced — the ONE interaction primitive, so the four human-in-the-loop shapes are
four control lists rather than four agents: an APPROVAL is two `button`s, an OPEN QUESTION is a
one-field `form`, a DRAFT REVIEW is a `form` whose `field` is prefilled with the draft (with a `button`
beside it to reject), and a MULTIPLE CHOICE is a `select`. Every control is live at once and the FIRST
answer settles the ask; the controls are then stripped from the message, so a second answer has nothing
to press. Branch on the control's own id — `case clicked(id => "approve", by => _)` — never on display
text.

Post to a channel whose MEMBERSHIP is the trust boundary: any member may answer. @by@ on the answer is the
answerer's raw Slack user id (an opaque `U…` id, not a name) — a workspace's ids are a small, guessable
space, so a plain digest of one is dictionary-reversible: pass it through `author_tag` before letting it
leave the program. That agent is this package's answer to a pseudonym every bot was otherwise writing
(and getting wrong) for itself: keyed with `crypto.hmac_sha256` under a named secret, so the tag cannot
be walked back to an account.

RUN `check_controls` WHERE THE CONTROLS ARE BUILT, not here. It answers every one of Slack's caps —
including the counts and the duplicate ids — as a VALUE, purely, with no connection needed: a gate's
constructor can refuse itself before a run ever starts. It is deliberately not wired into this agent:
`ask` returns an `answer` and has no room in that type for a verdict, so an internal check could only
THROW, and what a failed check means is the caller's decision.

The answered message and the `answer` name things DIFFERENTLY, each for its reader. The line left in the
channel keeps the control's own @label@ (for a `select`, the chosen option) and MENTIONS the answerer, so a
human scrolling back reads words and a name; the `answer` carries the @id@ the program chose and @by@ as
the raw user id, so the program gets keys it can branch on and correlate. That is why a label is worth
writing as an audit line: it is the half of the record a person will actually read.

Opening a `form`'s dialog and closing it again is NOT an answer: nothing was submitted, so the question
stays open and any control — that form again, or a sibling — can still answer it. A curious press cannot
consume the ask.

The ask holds NO time limit, deliberately: a deadline is `time.with_deadline` wrapped around it, and a
withdrawal is `region.cancel_by_id` on the fiber holding it. One blocking question composes with both,
whereas an expiry baked in here would make every caller handle a timeout it never asked for.

EVERY ending takes the controls off, not just an answered one, because a question nobody is waiting on any
more must not stay pressable: an answer leaves its own outcome line, a cancel or an expired deadline leaves
`(expired)`, and a question the platform broke leaves `(failed)`. All three are the same edit and all three
are BEST EFFORT — fire-and-forget, so no ending waits on a cosmetic post, and a failed edit is swallowed
rather than turned into the ask's outcome. Two endings genuinely cannot tidy up: a runtime restart (the
sidecar holding the prompt is gone) and a whole-run teardown (the provider's `finally` closes the client
before the edit lands). The everyday case — one arm of a `with_deadline` expiring while the connection stays
up — does tidy up.

A `form`'s inputs are NOT validated, at all and by design: every box is optional, a blank one comes back as
the empty string, and `submitted`'s @values@ is total over the declared fields. Nor COULD they be — the
socket acknowledges every interaction the instant it arrives, which is exactly what closes the dialog, so
this package can never answer a submission with per-field errors. Validate in the program and `ask` again.

The wait rides one external call, so a runtime restart while it is open interrupts it under the
at-most-once rule (a catchable panic) and leaves those controls stale, per above. That failure is the
DESIGNED outcome, not a defect to absorb here: let the panic ride to your supervisor and restart the asking
flow — whoever wanted the answer asks again — rather than guessing an answer that never landed.

Raises `slack_error` when a Slack call fails: posting the question, or opening a `form`'s dialog (its
three-second interaction token expired). A control past one of Slack's caps is that same failure — the
platform rejects the payload, surfacing as `api_error` — and a form's OWN caps (its title, its inputs) show
when the dialog opens, not when the question posts. Catch `api_error` to ask again.

Nothing here is CLAMPED, and nothing here can panic on a cap: this package renders a view as plain data
and hands it to Slack, so a string past one of the numbers on `button` / `select` / `field` / `form` is
Slack's rejection arriving as a typed `api_error` that the call site catches. The Discord twin clamps a
caption instead, because it renders through a client-side builder whose validators run in its own
sidecar. Write a portable control to the tighter of the two: a ≤24-character title, ≤45-character field
labels, ≤75-character button labels and options.

declarations.documentation:
Check @controls@ against Slack's caps LOCALLY and answer with a VALUE — `valid`, or `invalid`
carrying one sentence naming the offending control. Pure: no connection, no io, nothing to catch, so it
belongs where the controls are BUILT (a gate's constructor, a test) rather than where they are asked.

It is deliberately NOT wired into `ask`. `ask` returns an `answer`; there is no room in that type for a
verdict, so an internal check could only THROW, and a caller must be free to decide what a failed check
means: refuse the gate, shorten the label, ask anyway. The Discord twin took the same decision after an
outage in which a 67-character label restarted a resident system on every attempt.

WHAT IT REPORTS, and how that differs from the twin. Here EVERYTHING is fatal — Slack refuses the
payload, so a label past its cap and an id past its cap fail identically, and a BLANK label fails too
(an empty Block Kit `plain_text` is as illegal as an over-long one). The Discord twin has a second,
SILENT class to report — captions it would clamp — which this package cannot have, because it clamps
nothing. So a control that passes here posts as written, exactly:

- Every string on every control: an @id@, a @label@, a `select` placeholder or option, a `form` @title@,
  a `field` @label@ — blank or past its cap in `limits`.
- A `field`'s @value@: blank is legal (it is the absence of a prefill), over-long is fatal.
- The counts: a dropdown with no options or past @select_options@, a dialog with no boxes or past
  @form_fields@, more controls than the single actions row holds (@buttons_per_row@), and an EMPTY
  @controls@ — which Slack posts happily as a bare prompt that nobody can ever answer, so the ask waits
  forever.
- DUPLICATE ids, which nothing else catches usefully. Two controls sharing an `action_id` cannot be told
  apart on the way back — Slack returns the id and nothing more — so a press on one would answer as the
  other, "deny" answering as "approve". A `form`'s @fields@ are checked the same way, since
  `submitted.values` is keyed by field id and two boxes sharing one would collapse into a single entry.

Lengths are counted in Unicode code points, and Slack does not specify its own counting; a string within
a character or two of its cap should be shortened rather than argued about.

```katari
let controls = [slack.button(id = "approve", label = "Approve"), slack.button(id = "deny", label = "Deny")]
match (slack.check_controls(controls = controls)) {
  case slack.valid() -> slack.ask(channel = channel, prompt = prompt, controls = controls)
  case slack.invalid(reason => reason) -> refuse_to_open_the_gate(why = reason)
}
```

blank comes back as the empty string, so `submitted`'s @values@ is total over the form's declared fields.
A `field` carries no required-ness knob, so nothing here invents a check the program never asked for, and
clearing a prefilled draft stays a legitimate edit. Slack caps a box's label at 2000 characters and its
@id@ (an `action_id`) at 255, and rejects an over-cap dialog as `api_error` when it opens — a far more
generous label than the Discord twin's 45, which the twin CLAMPS; a `field` that must render on both
platforms is written to the shorter one.

verbatim (so a program may match the option itself — the options are its own strings). Slack caps the
placeholder at 150 characters, each option at 75, and the list at 100 options; over any of them Slack
rejects the payload as `api_error`.

and WHAT in one line — the first problem found, in declaration order, so a fix at a time converges.

distinct.

declarations.documentation:
Shorten @text@ so it fits in ONE Slack message, ending it with @marker@ when anything was cut — the
arithmetic every caller was doing against `limits()` by hand, and the half of that job which is
mechanical rather than editorial.

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY A SLICE. Past `limits()`'s @message_text@ Slack REFUSES an `ask`'s prompt (a
question is a section block, and an over-long block is `invalid_blocks` → `api_error`), so an over-long
prompt is a question that can never be asked — a gate that can never be granted, failing identically on
every retry. The room is therefore @message_text@ MINUS the marker's own length, because the marker is
part of what gets posted; measuring the text, cutting it to the cap and appending afterwards is the one
way this is got wrong, and it puts the result back over the cap every time.

It bounds against @message_text@ (3000) rather than @post_text@ (40000) DELIBERATELY, on both counts:
that is the number a prompt actually fails at, and it is the number the Discord twin's single cap
governs both planes with — so text fitted here fits there. A plain `send_message` may legitimately carry
more (Slack truncates it rather than refusing), and a caller who wants that reach bounds it by
@post_text@ itself.

WHY THE MARKER IS YOURS. Only the caller knows what the reader needs told, but SOMETHING must be told:
text that was silently docked reads exactly like text that ended, and a model reading it will answer
from a fragment as though it had the whole. Write the marker as the FACT — "… (cut: the first 2,900 of
7,400 characters)" — rather than as a bare ellipsis, so whoever reads it knows to ask for the rest.

Text that already fits comes back UNCHANGED, with no marker, so this is safe to wrap around everything.
A @marker@ that alone exceeds the cap leaves no room for any text and comes back cut to the cap itself:
the one guarantee here is that the result fits.

parameters.documentation: The text to fit; returned unchanged when it already does.

parameters.label: marker

marker.description: What to end the result with when anything was cut — your own words, saying that it was cut and ideally by how much.

text.description: The text to fit; returned unchanged when it already does.

declarations.documentation:
Tag a Slack user id into a short, stable PSEUDONYM — the ~25 lines every bot that lets a speaker reach
a model or a log was writing for itself, with the same one way to get it wrong. This package's own docs
used to INSTRUCT that hand-rolling, in two places, which is how it became clear it belonged here.

WHY NOT A PLAIN DIGEST. A `U…` id looks opaque but is not drawn from an opaque space: a workspace holds
some thousands of members at most, and Slack will hand any member's id to any app with `users:read` (or
simply to whoever reads a mention in a public channel), so the set of candidate ids is small, listable,
and often already known. `crypto.sha256` of one is therefore reversible by dictionary — anyone holding
the digest hashes the workspace's ids until one matches, and the pseudonym is a user id again.
`crypto.hmac_sha256` under a secret KEY has no such attack: without the key there is nothing to hash
candidates with. That is the whole difference between a pseudonym and an obfuscation, and it is one
function call wide, which is exactly why it kept being got wrong.

WHAT COMES OUT is safe to SHOW: @length@ hex characters (8 by default — 32 bits, opaque and short enough
to sit inline in a prompt or a log line), stable for as long as the key is, and meaningless to anyone
without the key. Rotating the key rotates every pseudonym, which is the intended way to sever a
correlation. Keep @length@ generous if the tag must be UNIQUE rather than merely readable: 8 hex
characters collide at around 2^16 distinct speakers by the birthday bound, so a full 64 is what a program
correlating abuse reports across a large workspace should carry, and a short one is what it shows. The
result is deliberately PUBLIC despite the private key — an HMAC reveals nothing about its key, which is
the sound declassification `crypto.hmac_sha256` documents.

THE KEY is named, not passed: a `credentials.source` (`credentials.env(key = ...)` or
`credentials.oauth(name = ...)`), so the secret's VALUE never enters the app's dataflow. It resolves at
EVERY call, like every other credential use in Katari, so a rotated key lands without a restart — a bot
tagging every message pays one credential read per message for that. Any secret with a stable lifetime
will do; the bot token (`SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`) is the usual choice, since it already exists and dies with the
bot's identity. Tags do not carry across the Discord twin even under the same key — the two hash
different id spaces — so one person on both platforms is two pseudonyms, which is the honest answer
rather than a defect.

WHAT IT IS NOT is an anonymisation. A pseudonym is stable by construction, so it links everything one
person ever said; what it removes is the ability to turn that link back into an account. Whether even a
pseudonymous link may cross to an AI provider is the app's judgement — this agent only makes the tag
correct.

escalation instead.)
